rows.title: AI
rows.contest: Whether artificial intelligence should be built and deployed as fast as possible to capture its benefits, or slowed and controlled until its risks are better understood.
rows.stakes: The argument turns on whether machines that mimic human judgment can be trusted with decisions that affect jobs, safety, and truth itself. It also turns on who gets to set the rules, the companies building the systems, the government, or someone else, and who benefits when those rules are written.

objects.title: Sherman Antitrust Act
objects.author: U.S. Congress
objects.about: This is a federal law passed by the U.S. Congress in 1890. It bans contracts, combinations, and conspiracies that restrain trade, and it bans monopolization of trade or commerce. It became the legal foundation for later antitrust cases against large companies.

objects.title: Telecommunications Act of 1996
objects.author: U.S. Congress
objects.about: The Telecommunications Act of 1996 is a federal law passed by the U.S. Congress and signed by President Clinton on February 8, 1996. It rewrote federal rules for telephone, cable, and broadcast companies, including limits on how many stations one company could own.

objects.title: USA PATRIOT Act
objects.author: U.S. Congress
objects.about: Congress passed this law, Public Law 107-56, and the president signed it on 26 October 2001, soon after the terrorist attacks of that year. It widened the government's powers to investigate terrorism and to collect information, including electronic communications.

objects.title: General Data Protection Regulation
objects.author: European Parliament and Council
objects.about: This is a regulation passed by the European Parliament and Council in 2016. It sets rules for how organizations collect, store, and use personal data of people in the European Union. It also grants individuals rights over their own data, such as access and deletion.

objects.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (the AI Act)
objects.author: European Parliament and Council
objects.about: This is a regulation adopted by the European Parliament and Council in 2024. It sets rules for the development and use of artificial intelligence systems across the European Union, including requirements based on risk level. It is described as the first comprehensive law on AI now in force in Europe.

objects.title: Executive Order 14179: Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence
objects.author: Donald J. Trump
objects.about: This is an executive order signed by Donald J. Trump in 2025 and published in the Federal Register. It reverses the prior administration's 2023 order on AI policy. It marks a shift in the federal government's approach to regulating artificial intelligence in the United States.

beginnings.line: Congress passed the Sherman Antitrust Act to outlaw monopolies and restraints on trade.
Congress rewrote the nation's communications law in 1996, covering telephone, cable and broadcast, and for the first time the internet.
Congress passed the USA PATRIOT Act soon after the terrorist attacks of that year, widening the government's powers to investigate and watch people.
The European Parliament and Council adopted the General Data Protection Regulation to govern personal data handling.
The European Parliament and Council enacted Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, known as the AI Act, to regulate artificial intelligence.
President Trump signed an executive order removing barriers to American leadership in artificial intelligence.

rows.title: Inflation
rows.contest: Whether rising prices are mainly a temporary shock the Fed and government should ride out and cushion, or a lasting loss of purchasing power that demands tighter money and a firm response.
rows.stakes: Open questions include whether people come to accept high prices as normal, when central bankers must act, and by whom relief is delivered. It also asks whether wages can catch up, and who gains or loses when paychecks and benefits trail prices.

rows.title: Robots and Law
rows.contest: Whether existing laws written for human hands and intent can cover harm done through machines, or whether new rules are needed for what robots do in public.
rows.stakes: Who is responsible when a machine acts, the person who owns it, the one who steers it, or the one who built it? When do courts and police treat a machine's movements as someone's intent, and who decides?
